notes.definition: Classification is the sorting of living organisms into groups. Linnaeus grouped organisms by structure and characteristics into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species; chemical analysis has since led to Carl Woese's three-domain system of archaea, bacteria and eukaryota.
explanation: Traditionally, living things have been classified into groups depending on their structure and characteristics, in a system developed by Carl Linnaeus in the 18th century. Organisms that share more features are placed in the same smaller groups. Classification helps scientists to identify organisms, to communicate clearly about them and to understand how they are related.

Linnaeus classified living things into a hierarchy of groups. From largest to smallest these are: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Each group contains several smaller groups. For example, the lion is in the kingdom Animalia (animals), phylum Chordata, class Mammalia (mammals), order Carnivora, family Felidae (cats), genus Panthera and species leo. The further down the hierarchy two organisms share a group, the more features they have in common and the more closely related they are. A useful way to remember the order is 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'.

Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species. The lion is Panthera leo and the tiger is Panthera tigris: both are in the genus Panthera, so they are closely related, but they are different species. The genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name with a lower-case letter, and the name is written in italics (or underlined when handwritten). Binomial names are the same in every country and language, so they avoid the confusion caused by common names.

Developments in biology have changed classification systems. As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed. For example, electron microscopes showed the internal structure of cells, revealing that prokaryotic cells (with no nucleus) are very different from eukaryotic cells. This led to a model with five kingdoms: animals, plants, fungi, protists and prokaryotes.

Due to evidence available from chemical analysis, there is now a three-domain system developed by Carl Woese. Chemical analysis showed that some organisms that look like bacteria are actually very different from them. In this system organisms are divided into three domains: archaea (primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments, such as hot springs and very salty lakes), bacteria (true bacteria), and eukaryota (which includes protists, fungi, plants and animals). The domain is a level above kingdom.

Evolutionary trees are a method used by scientists to show how they believe organisms are related. They use current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms. Branch points represent common ancestors; the more recently two groups share a common ancestor, the more closely related they are.
keyFacts: Linnaeus classified living things by their structure and characteristics.
Linnaean groups, largest to smallest: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species, e.g. Homo sapiens.
The genus name has a capital letter; the species name is lower case.
Improvements in microscopes revealed internal structures, and understanding of biochemistry grew, so new models of classification were proposed.
Carl Woese developed the three-domain system, based on evidence from chemical analysis.
Archaea: primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments.
Eukaryota: includes protists, fungi, plants and animals.
Evolutionary trees use current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.

keyTerms.definition: Sorting living organisms into groups based on shared features.
Carl Linnaeus's system that classifies organisms into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species based on structure and characteristics.
Naming each species with two words: its genus followed by its species, e.g. Panthera leo.
A group of closely related species; the first part of a binomial name.
The smallest group in classification; organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. The second part of a binomial name.
The highest level of classification in the three-domain system: archaea, bacteria or eukaryota.
A domain of primitive bacteria, usually living in extreme environments.
The domain of organisms whose cells have a nucleus: protists, fungi, plants and animals.
A diagram showing how scientists believe organisms are related, using classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.

workedExamples.title: Using binomial names to judge relatedness
workedExamples.question: The grey wolf is Canis lupus, the coyote is Canis latrans and the red fox is Vulpes vulpes. Which two are most closely related? Explain.
steps: The first word of a binomial name is the genus.
The grey wolf and the coyote are both in the genus Canis.
The red fox is in a different genus, Vulpes.
Organisms in the same genus share more features and a more recent common ancestor.
workedExamples.answer: The grey wolf and the coyote, because they are in the same genus (Canis).

workedExamples.title: Placing an organism in the Linnaean hierarchy
workedExamples.question: Humans are classified as: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens. Name the class, the family and the binomial name of humans.
steps: Match the groups to the order kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Class is the third group: Mammalia.
Family is the fifth group: Hominidae.
Binomial name = genus + species = Homo sapiens (genus capitalised, species lower case).
workedExamples.answer: Class: Mammalia. Family: Hominidae. Binomial name: Homo sapiens.

workedExamples.title: Placing organisms in the three-domain system
workedExamples.question: Put each organism in its domain: a mushroom; a microorganism living in a hot spring at 90 °C that looks like a bacterium but is chemically very different; E. coli; an oak tree.
steps: A mushroom is a fungus, so it is a eukaryote: Eukaryota.
A primitive bacterium-like organism in an extreme environment is in Archaea.
E. coli is a true bacterium: Bacteria.
An oak tree is a plant: Eukaryota.
workedExamples.answer: Mushroom: Eukaryota. Hot spring organism: Archaea. E. coli: Bacteria. Oak tree: Eukaryota.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the binomial name is the kingdom and species, or the family and species.
misconceptions.right: In fact, it is always genus then species, e.g. Homo sapiens.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think archaea are just ordinary bacteria.
misconceptions.right: In fact, chemical analysis showed archaea are so different from true bacteria that Woese put them in a separate domain.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think classification systems are fixed and never change.
misconceptions.right: In fact, new evidence from better microscopes and chemical analysis has led to new models, such as the three-domain system.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fungi are plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact, fungi are a separate kingdom. They do not photosynthesise. They are in the domain Eukaryota along with plants, animals and protists.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think organisms that look similar must be closely related.
misconceptions.right: In fact, appearance can mislead. Chemical analysis and internal structures give stronger evidence of relationships.

realWorld: Scientists all over the world use binomial names, so a researcher in Japan and one in Brazil know they are studying the same species.
Enzymes from archaea that live in hot springs are used in laboratories because they work at high temperatures, for example in copying DNA.
Conservation organisations use classification to decide which species are most distinct and in need of protection.
examTips: Learn the order kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species with a mnemonic such as 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'.
The binomial name is genus + species. The genus has a capital letter, the species does not.
Learn the three domains with their descriptions: archaea (primitive bacteria in extreme environments), bacteria (true bacteria), eukaryota (protists, fungi, plants, animals).
When asked why classification has changed, mention improved microscopes (internal structures) and chemical / biochemical analysis.
When using information to compare organisms, find the smallest group they share: the smaller the shared group, the more closely related they are.
summary: Linnaeus classified organisms by structure and characteristics.
Groups: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Binomial names use genus and species, e.g. Panthera leo.
Better microscopes and biochemistry led to new classification models.
Woese's three-domain system: archaea, bacteria, eukaryota, based on chemical analysis.
Evolutionary trees use classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct ones.

questions.question: Which scientist developed the traditional system of classifying living things by their structure and characteristics?
markScheme: 1 mark: Carl Linnaeus
questions.explanation: Linnaeus developed the traditional system. Woese developed the newer three-domain system, Darwin proposed natural selection and Mendel studied inheritance.

questions.question: Which is the largest group in the Linnaean system of classification?
markScheme: 1 mark: kingdom
questions.explanation: Kingdom is the largest Linnaean group and species is the smallest.

questions.question: The binomial name of an organism is made of which two groups?
markScheme: 1 mark: genus and species
questions.explanation: Binomial means 'two names': genus then species, as in Homo sapiens.

questions.question: Which shows the Linnaean groups in the correct order from largest to smallest?
options: Kingdom, class, phylum, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, phylum, class, family, order, genus, species
Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, phylum, order, class, family, species, genus
markScheme: 1 mark: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
questions.explanation: The other options each swap two groups. 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup' helps you remember the correct order.

questions.question: Who developed the three-domain system of classification?
markScheme: 1 mark: Carl Woese
questions.explanation: Carl Woese developed the three-domain system using evidence from chemical analysis. Do not confuse him with Carl Linnaeus.

questions.question: What are the three domains in Woese's system?
markScheme: 1 mark: Archaea, Bacteria, Eukaryota
questions.explanation: Animals, plants and fungi are all within Eukaryota. Viruses are not placed in any of the three domains.

questions.question: In which domain are fungi placed?
markScheme: 1 mark: Eukaryota
questions.explanation: Eukaryota includes protists, fungi, plants and animals. 'Plants' is a kingdom, not a domain, and fungi are not plants.

questions.question: Which description best fits the archaea?
options: Organisms whose cells have a nucleus
Primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments
markScheme: 1 mark: primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments
questions.explanation: This is the specification description of archaea. Cells with a nucleus are eukaryotes, and archaea are not viruses or fungi.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the binomial names of two big cats.
What is the smallest group that both animals belong to?
markScheme: 1 mark: genus
questions.explanation: Both names start with Panthera, the genus. They are different species. They also share family and kingdom, but those are larger groups.

questions.question: What type of evidence led to the development of the three-domain system?
markScheme: 1 mark: chemical analysis
questions.explanation: Chemical analysis revealed that archaea are very different from true bacteria, even though they look similar.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why new models of classification have been proposed since Linnaeus's time?
options: Organisms have changed their appearance since the 18th century
Linnaeus classified organisms only by their colour
Scientists decided that seven groups were too many
Improved microscopes revealed internal structures and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed
markScheme: 1 mark: improved microscopes revealed internal structures and understanding of biochemical processes progressed
questions.explanation: New evidence, not changes in organisms, led to new models. Linnaeus used many structural characteristics, not only colour.

questions.explanation: Evolutionary trees use current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms. An extinct organism has no living individuals to study.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows part of the classification of the lion and the domestic cat.
Which statement about the lion and the domestic cat must be true?
options: They are in the same order
They are in the same species
They have the same binomial name
markScheme: 1 mark: they are in the same order
questions.explanation: Each family belongs to one order, so the lion and domestic cat, which share the family Felidae, must share the order, class, phylum and kingdom. Different genera means different species and different binomial names.

questions.question: Humans have the binomial name Homo sapiens. State the genus of humans.
markScheme: 1 mark: Homo
questions.explanation: The first word of the binomial name is the genus; the second (sapiens) is the species.

questions.question: Name the two groups used in the binomial system, in the order they are written.
markScheme: 1 mark: genus (first)
1 mark: species (second)
questions.explanation: Binomial names are always written genus first, then species.

questions.question: Name the domain that contains plants and animals.
markScheme: 1 mark: Eukaryota
questions.explanation: Plants and animals have cells with a nucleus, so they are eukaryotes.

questions.question:
Write these groups in order of size, from the largest to the smallest.
family     kingdom     species     order
markScheme: 1 mark: kingdom, order, family, species
questions.explanation: In the full list (kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species), order comes before family.

questions.question: Explain why scientists use binomial names rather than common names for organisms.
markScheme: 1 mark: common names vary between countries / languages, or one common name may be used for different species
1 mark: binomial names are the same worldwide, so they avoid confusion / help scientists communicate
questions.explanation: For example, 'robin' means different birds in Britain and North America, but each has a unique binomial name.

questions.question: Describe the organisms in the domain Archaea.
markScheme: 1 mark: primitive bacteria
1 mark: usually living in extreme environments (e.g. hot springs, very salty water)
questions.explanation: Archaea look like bacteria but chemical analysis shows they are very different.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the binomial names of two species of beetle.
What does Table 1 tell you about how these two beetles are related?
markScheme: 1 mark: they are closely related / share many characteristics
1 mark: they share a recent common ancestor / they are also in the same family, order, class, phylum and kingdom
questions.explanation: Both names start with Carabus, so they are in the same genus. Genus is the smallest group above species, so sharing a genus means a close relationship and a recent common ancestor.

questions.question: Explain how improvements in microscopes affected the classification of living organisms.
markScheme: 1 mark: microscopes revealed internal structures (e.g. of cells: whether they have a nucleus)
1 mark: so organisms could be grouped using this new evidence and new models of classification were proposed (e.g. prokaryotes separated from eukaryotes)
questions.explanation: Linnaeus could only use features visible to the eye or simple lenses. Electron microscopes showed differences in cell structure that led to new groups.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the classification of three animals. All three are in the family Canidae.
Which two animals are the most closely related?
Explain your answer.

questions.question: Describe the Linnaean system of classification and how organisms are named in this system.
markScheme: Indicative content: developed by Carl Linnaeus; organisms classified into groups based on their structure and characteristics; groups in order: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; each group contains smaller groups; organisms in smaller shared groups have more features in common; binomial system of naming using genus and species; genus has a capital letter, species lower case, written in italics / underlined; example such as Homo sapiens or Panthera leo.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): the hierarchy described accurately in order and the binomial system explained with an example.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some groups named or the binomial system mentioned, with little detail.
questions.explanation: Cover both parts: the seven groups in order, and binomial naming with a correctly written example.

questions.question: Describe how, and explain why, systems for classifying living organisms have changed since the time of Linnaeus.
markScheme: Indicative content: Linnaeus classified organisms by structure and characteristics (what could be seen); hierarchy of kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; binomial naming; as microscopes improved, evidence of internal structures (e.g. cell structure, presence of a nucleus) became available; organisms were reclassified, e.g. into five kingdoms (animals, plants, fungi, protists, prokaryotes); understanding of biochemical processes progressed; chemical analysis showed some organisms that look alike are very different; Carl Woese developed the three-domain system; archaea (primitive bacteria usually in extreme environments), bacteria (true bacteria), eukaryota (protists, fungi, plants, animals); domain is above kingdom; evolutionary trees now combine classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct ones; classification now reflects evolutionary relationships more accurately.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered description of the changes linked clearly to the new evidence (microscopes and chemical analysis), including accurate details of the three-domain system.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes changes with some explanation of why, or describes the three-domain system with limited explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about Linnaeus or the three domains, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Link each change to the evidence that caused it: microscopes revealed internal structures, and chemical analysis led to the three domains. Give the three domains with their descriptions.

questions.question: Compare the Linnaean system of classification with the three-domain system.
markScheme: Indicative content. Similarities: both sort organisms into groups based on shared features; both use a hierarchy; species and binomial names still used within the three-domain system. Differences: Linnaean system developed by Linnaeus, three-domain by Carl Woese; Linnaean based on structure and characteristics (what can be observed), three-domain based on evidence from chemical analysis; three-domain adds a level above kingdom; three-domain separates archaea from true bacteria, which Linnaean-style systems grouped together or did not recognise; three domains are archaea, bacteria and eukaryota (protists, fungi, plants, animals).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least one similarity and two differences, clearly compared.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): facts about one or both systems with little direct comparison.
questions.explanation: A compare question needs points about both systems side by side. The key difference is the type of evidence: structure and characteristics against chemical analysis.
